		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Trust and Financial Services</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">MutualWealth and MutualFinancial are the wealth management and investment services divisions of the Bank that provide a variety of fee-based financial services, including trust and estate administration, investment management services, &nbsp;life insurance, broker advisory services, retirement plan administration and private banking services, in our market areas. &nbsp;Trust services are provided to both individual and corporate customers, including personal trust and agency accounts, employee benefit plans and corporate bond trustee accounts.&nbsp;The market value of managed and non-managed fiduciary assets at December 31, 2018 were $361.5 million and $133.5 million, respectively. &nbsp;These activities provide a significant source of fee income to the Company and in 2018 constituted 24.9% of the Company&#x2019;s non-interest income.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Subsidiary and Other Activities</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The Company, as a bank holding company that has elected to be treated as a financial holding company, is allowed to engage in activities and invest in subsidiaries as authorized by Federal law and the regulations of the FRB. &nbsp;At December&nbsp;31, 2018, the Company had an active captive insurance company, MutualFirst Risk Management,&nbsp;Inc. and another subsidiary, Mutual Risk Advisors, an information security consulting firm.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">As an Indiana commercial bank, MutualBank is allowed to invest in subsidiaries as authorized by Indiana law and the IDFI. &nbsp;Under federal law and FDIC regulations, those subsidiaries generally may engage as principal only in activities that are permissible for national bank subsidiaries, unless the Bank receives FDIC approval to engage in other activities permitted by Indiana law and the IDFI. &nbsp;Activities engaged in as agent, including insurance agency activities, are not subject to this limitation.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, MutualBank had an active investment subsidiary, Mutual Federal Investment Company, which is a Nevada corporation that holds and manages a portion of MutualBank&#x2019;s investment portfolio. &nbsp;As of December&nbsp;31, 2018, the market value of securities managed was $355.7 million. &nbsp;Mutual Federal Investment Company has one active subsidiary, Mutual Federal REIT,&nbsp;Inc., which is a Maryland corporation holding approximately $48.1 million in consumer closed end first mortgage loans.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The Bank had one other active subsidiary as of December&nbsp;31, 2018. &nbsp;Summit Service Corporation which controls the 100% wholly owned active subsidiary, Summit Mortgage,&nbsp;Inc., which is an Indiana corporation that originates and sells consumer closed end first mortgage loans. &nbsp;As of December&nbsp;31, 2018, Summit Mortgage had $3.1 million in loans held for sale.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Employees</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, we had a total of 485 full-time and 43 part-time employees. &nbsp;Our employees are not represented by any collective bargaining group. &nbsp;Management considers its employee relations to be good.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">How We Are Regulated</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">MutualFirst Financial is a financial holding company subject to FRB regulation, and MutualBank is an Indiana commercial bank subject to regulation by the IDFI and the FDIC. &nbsp;The Dodd-Frank Act created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (&#x201C;CFPB&#x201D;), which has authority to promulgate regulations intended to protect consumers with respect to financial products and services, including those provided by the Bank, and to restrict unfair, deceptive or abusive conduct by providers of consumer financial products and services. &nbsp;The FDIC examines the Bank for compliance with these regulations. &nbsp;As a public company, the Company is subject to the regulation and reporting requirements of the SEC.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;">27</font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#TOC"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Set forth below is a brief description of certain laws and regulations that apply to us. &nbsp;This description, as well as other descriptions of laws and regulations contained in this Form&nbsp;10&#8209;K, is not complete and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the applicable laws and regulations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Legislation is introduced from time to time in the United States Congress and the Indiana General Assembly that may affect our operations. &nbsp;In addition, the regulations governing the Company and the Bank may be amended from time to time by the IDFI, FDIC, CFPB, FRB or SEC, as appropriate. &nbsp;Legislation enacted in 2018 and summarized below may reduce some of the burden&#x2019;s associated with the implementation of the Dodd-Frank Act, but the actual impact of the policies related to the Dodd Frank Act reforms is impossible to predict with any certainty.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">2018 Regulatory Reform</font><font style="display:inline;">.&nbsp;&nbsp;In May 2018 the Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief and Consumer Protection Act (the &#x201C;Act&#x201D;) was enacted to modify or remove certain financial reform rules and regulations, including some of those implemented under the Dodd-Frank Act.&nbsp;&nbsp;While the Act maintains most of the regulatory structure established by the Dodd-Frank Act, it amends certain aspects of the regulatory framework for small depository institutions with assets of less than $10 billion and for large banks with assets of more than $50 billion.&nbsp;&nbsp;Many of these changes could result in meaningful regulatory relief for community banks such as MutualBank.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">&nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The Act, among other matters, expands the definition of qualified mortgages which may be held by a financial institution and simplifies the regulatory capital rules for financial institutions and their holding companies with total consolidated assets of less than $10 billion by instructing the federal banking regulators to establish a single &#x201C;Community Bank Leverage Ratio&#x201D; of between 8 and 10 percent to replace the leverage and risk-based regulatory capital ratios.&nbsp;&nbsp;The Act also expands the category of holding companies that may rely on the &#x201C;Small Bank Holding Company and Savings and Loan Holding Company Policy statement&#x201D; by raising the maximum amount of assets a qualifying holding company may have from $1.0 billion to $3.0 billion.&nbsp;&nbsp;This expansion also excludes such holding companies from the minimum capital requirement of the Dodd-Frank Act.&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, the Act includes regulatory relief for community banks regarding regulatory examination cycles, call reports, the Volcker Rule (proprietary trading prohibitions), mortgage disclosures and risk weights for certain high-risk commercial real estate loans.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;"> &nbsp; &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">It is difficult at this time to predict when or how any new standards under the Act will ultimately be applied to us or what specific impact the Act and the yet to be written implementing rules and regulations will have on community banks.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">MutualFirst Financial</font><font style="display:inline;">. &nbsp;MutualFirst Financial is a bank holding company that has elected to be treated as a financial holding company. &nbsp;MutualFirst is required to register and file reports with the FRB and is subject to regulation and examination by the FRB, including requirements that the Company serve as a source of financial and managerial strength for the Bank, particularly if the Bank is in financial distress. &nbsp;In addition, the FRB has enforcement authority over the Company and any of its non-bank subsidiaries. &nbsp;The Company&#x2019;s direct activities and those of its non-bank subsidiaries are subject to FRB regulation and must be activities permissible for a bank holding company, or for a financial holding company &nbsp;(generally securities and insurance activities). &nbsp;The Company must obtain FRB approval to acquire substantially all the assets of another bank or bank holding company or to merge with another bank holding company. &nbsp;In addition, the Company must obtain FRB authorization to control more than 5% of the shares of any other bank or bank holding company and may not own more than 5% of any other entity engaged in activities not permitted for the Company. &nbsp;The IDFI also has certain oversight authority over the Company, including acquisitions of banks and bank holding companies. &nbsp;The FRB imposes consolidated capital requirements on the Company. &nbsp;See &#x201C;- Regulatory Capital Requirements.&#x201D;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">MutualBank</font><font style="display:inline;">. &nbsp;As an Indiana commercial bank, MutualBank is subject to regulation, examination and supervision by the IDFI. &nbsp;Indiana and Federal laws regulate many aspects of the Bank&#x2019;s operations including branching, dividends, interest and fees collected, anti-money laundering activities, confidentiality </font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">To fund its operations, the IDFI has established a schedule for the assessment of supervisory fees for all Indiana financial institutions. &nbsp;These supervisory fees are computed based on the Bank&#x2019;s total assets and trust assets and increase if the Bank experiences financial distress. The IDFI also charges fees for certain applications and other filings.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">FDIC Regulation and Insurance of Accounts</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">As a state-chartered, non-member bank, MutualBank is subject to regulation, examination and supervision by the FDIC. &nbsp;The FDIC does not assess fees for its examination and supervision of the Bank. &nbsp;The FDIC oversees the Bank&#x2019;s operations under federal law, regulations and policies, including consumer compliance laws, and ensures that the Bank operates in a safe and sound manner. &nbsp;It regulates the Bank&#x2019;s branching, transactions with affiliates (including the Company) and loans to insiders. &nbsp;Under FDIC regulations, the Bank generally is prohibited from acquiring or owning any equity investments impermissible for national banks and from engaging as principal in activities that are not permitted for national banks without FDIC approval. &nbsp;During examinations, the FDIC may require the Bank to establish additional reserves for loan losses, which would decrease the Company&#x2019;s net income. &nbsp;The FDIC has adopted guidelines establishing safety and soundness standards on such matters as loan underwriting and documentation, asset quality, earnings standards, internal controls and audit systems, interest rate risk exposure and compensation and other employee benefits. &nbsp;Any institution that fails to comply with these standards must submit a compliance plan.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The Bank&#x2019;s deposits are insured up to the applicable limits by the FDIC, and such insurance is backed by the full faith and credit of the United States Government. &nbsp;The basic deposit insurance level is $250,000 per each separately insured depositor, as defined in FDIC regulations. &nbsp;As insurer, the FDIC imposes deposit insurance premiums and is authorized to conduct examinations of and to require reporting by FDIC-insured institutions. &nbsp;Our deposit insurance premiums for the&nbsp;year ended December&nbsp;31, 2018 were $898,000. &nbsp;The FDIC&#x2019;s premiums may increase if the Bank&#x2019;s regulatory capital or supervisory ratings deteriorate.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">In accordance with the Dodd-Frank Act, the FDIC has issued regulations setting insurance premium assessments based on an institution&#x2019;s total assets minus its Tier 1 capital instead of its deposits. &nbsp;The Bank&#x2019;s FDIC premiums are based on its supervisory ratings and certain financial ratios. &nbsp;Federal law requires that the reserve ratio of the FDIC deposit insurance fund be at least 1.35% by September&nbsp;2020. On September 30, 2018, the Deposit Insurance Fund Reserve Ratio reached 1.36%, exceeding the required minimum reserve ratio. This provides for depository institutions with total consolidated assets of $10 billion or less to receive assessment credits for the portion of their assessments that contributed to the growth in the reserve ratio from between 1.15% and 1.35%, to be applied when the reserve ratio is at or above 1.38%.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The FDIC may prohibit the Bank from engaging in any activity that it determines by regulation or order to pose a serious risk to the deposit insurance fund and may terminate our deposit insurance if it determines that we have engaged in unsafe or unsound practices or are in an unsafe or unsound condition.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Regulatory Capital Requirements</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">MutualBank is&nbsp;required to maintain a minimum level of regulatory capital. &nbsp;The FDIC has established capital standards for the Bank. &nbsp;The FDIC also may impose capital requirements in excess of these standards on individual institutions on a case-by-case basis. &nbsp;Financial institutions are expected to maintain a level of capital adequate with the risk profile assigned to their assets in accordance with the guidelines. See &#x201C;Item&nbsp;7&nbsp;- Management&#x2019;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operation&nbsp;- Capital Resources&#x201D; for information on the Bank&#x2019;s compliance with these capital requirements.</font>
		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The current capital regulations of the FDIC became effective at the beginning of 2015 (with some changes phased in over several&nbsp;years). &nbsp;The capital regulations establish required minimum ratio for common equity Tier 1 (&#x201C;CET1&#x201D;) capital, Tier 1 capital and total capital and the minimum leverage ratio; establish risk-weightings for assets and certain off-balance sheet items for purposes of the risk-based capital ratios; require an additional capital conservation buffer over the minimum risk-based capital ratios; and define what qualifies as capital for purposes of meeting the capital requirements.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The minimum capital ratios are: (1)&nbsp;a CET1 capital ratio of 4.5% of risk-weighted assets; (2)&nbsp;a Tier 1 capital ratio of 6.0% of risk-weighted assets; (3)&nbsp;a total capital ratio of 8.0% of risk-weighted assets; and (4)&nbsp;a leverage ratio (the ratio of Tier 1 capital to average total adjusted assets) of 4.0%. &nbsp;CET1 generally consists of common stock; retained earnings; accumulated other comprehensive income (&#x201C;AOCI&#x201D;) except in the case of banking organizations that have elected to exclude AOCI from regulatory capital, as discussed below; and certain minority interests; all subject to applicable regulatory adjustments and deductions.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">There are a number of changes in what constitutes regulatory capital compared to earlier regulations, subject to transition periods. &nbsp;These changes include the phasing-out of certain instruments as qualifying capital. &nbsp;Mortgage servicing and deferred tax assets over designated&nbsp;percentages of CET1 are deducted from capital. &nbsp;In addition, Tier 1 capital includes AOCI, which includes all unrealized gains and losses on available for sale debt and equity securities. &nbsp;Because of our asset size, we had the one-time option of deciding in the first quarter of 2015 whether to permanently opt-out of the inclusion of unrealized gains and losses on available for sale debt and equity securities in our capital calculations. &nbsp;We made the decision to opt out.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The capital regulations changed in the risk-weighting of certain assets to better reflect credit risk and other risk exposure compared to earlier regulations. These changes include a 150% risk weight (up from 100%) for certain high volatility commercial real estate acquisition, development and construction loans and for non-residential mortgage loans that are 90&nbsp;days past due or otherwise in nonaccrual status; a 20% (up from 0%) credit conversion factor for the unused portion of a commitment with an original maturity of one&nbsp;year or less that is not unconditionally cancellable (set at 0%); and a 250% risk weight (up from 100%) for mortgage servicing and deferred tax assets that are not deducted from capital.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">In &nbsp;addition to the minimum CET1, Tier 1 and total capital ratios, the capital regulations require a capital conservation buffer consisting of additional CET1 capital greater than 2.5% of risk-weighted assets above the required minimum risk-based in order to avoid limitations on paying dividends, engaging in share repurchases and paying discretionary bonuses. The phase-in of the capital conservation buffer requirement began on January&nbsp;1, 2016, when a buffer greater than 0.625% of risk-weighted assets was required, which amount increases each&nbsp;year until the buffer requirement is fully implemented on January&nbsp;1, 2019.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Under the FDIC&#x2019;s prompt corrective action standards, in order to be considered well-capitalized, the Bank must have a ratio of CET1 capital to risk-weighted assets of 6.5%, a ratio of Tier 1 capital to risk-weighted assets of 8%, a ratio of total capital to risk-weighted assets of 10%, and a leverage ratio of 5%; and in order to be considered adequately capitalized, it must have the minimum capital ratios described above. &nbsp;To be considered well-capitalized a bank holding company must have, on a consolidated basis, at least a Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio of 8% and a total risk-based capital ratio of 10% and not be subject to a higher enforceable individualized capital requirement.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Section 201 of the Act requires the Federal banking agencies to promulgate a rule establishing a new &#x201C;Community Bank Leverage Ratio&#x201D; of 8%-10% for depository institutions and depository institution holding companies, with less than $10 billion in total consolidated assets. If such a depository institution or holding company maintains tangible equity in excess of this leverage ratio, it would be deemed to be in compliance with (1) the leverage and risk-based capital requirements promulgated by the Federal </font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;">30</font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#TOC"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;">banking agencies; (2) in the case of a depository institution, the capital ratio requirements to be considered &#x201C;well capitalized&#x201D; under the Federal banking agencies&#x2019; &#x201C;prompt corrective action&#x201D; regime; and (3) &#x201C;any other capital or leverage requirements to which the depository institution or holding company is subject, in each case unless the appropriate Federal banking agency determines otherwise based on the particular institution&#x2019;s risk profile. In carrying out these requirements, the Federal banking agencies are required to consult with State banking regulators and notify the applicable State banking regulator of any qualifying community bank that exceeds or no longer exceeds the Community Bank Leverage Ratio. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Limitations on Dividends and Other Capital Distributions</font><font style="display:inline;">. &nbsp;The Company&#x2019;s major source of funds consists of dividends from the Bank. &nbsp;The ability of the Bank to pay dividends depends on its earnings and capital levels and may be limited by FDIC or IDFI regulations, directives or orders, or by the capital conservation buffer requirements. &nbsp;In addition, under Indiana law, the Bank may pay dividends from undivided profits; however, in some circumstances it may be required to obtain IDFI approval of a dividend if the total dividends declared during the current&nbsp;year, including the proposed dividend, exceeds net income for the current&nbsp;year and retained net income for the prior two&nbsp;years, which excludes dividends paid during those&nbsp;years. The approval from IDFI is not required if the Bank meets exemption guidelines that mandate minimums for examination ratings and the Tier 1 leverage capital ratio, and the Bank is not subject to corrective action or supervisory order agreements. &nbsp;Since the Bank became regulated by the IDFI, it has been exempt from the pre-approval requirements. &nbsp;It is the Bank&#x2019;s policy to maintain a strong capital position, so, in times of financial or economic distress, the Bank will be less likely to pay dividends to the Company.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The ability of the Company to pay dividends to its stockholders is primarily dependent on the receipt of dividends from the Bank. &nbsp;Under Maryland law, the Company cannot pay cash dividends if it would render the Company unable to pay its debts or would be insolvent (unless they are paid from recent earnings).</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The FRB has issued a policy statement on the payment of cash dividends by bank holding companies, which expresses the FRB&#x2019;s view that a bank holding company should pay cash dividends only to the extent that its net income for the past&nbsp;year is sufficient to cover both the cash dividends and a rate of earnings retention that is consistent with the holding company&#x2019;s capital needs, asset quality and overall financial condition. &nbsp;The FRB also indicated that it would be inappropriate for a company experiencing serious financial problems to borrow funds to pay dividends. &nbsp;Furthermore, a bank holding company may be prohibited from paying any dividends if the holding company&#x2019;s bank subsidiary is not adequately capitalized. &nbsp;The payment of dividends by a bank or a bank holding company can also be restricted under the capital conversation buffer requirements in the capital regulations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">A bank holding company is required to give the FRB prior written notice of any purchase or redemption of its outstanding equity securities if the gross consideration for the purchase or redemption, when combined with the net consideration paid for all such purchases or redemptions during the preceding 12&nbsp;months, is equal to 10% or more of the company&#x2019;s consolidated net worth. &nbsp;The FRB may disapprove such a purchase or redemption if it determines that the proposal would constitute an unsafe or unsound practice or would violate any law, regulation, FRB order, or any condition imposed by, or written agreement with, the FRB. &nbsp;This notification requirement does not apply to any company that meets the well-capitalized standard for bank holding companies, is well-managed, and is not subject to any unresolved supervisory issues.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Federal Securities Laws</font><font style="display:inline;">. &nbsp;The common stock of the Company is registered with the SEC under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the &#x201C;Exchange Act&#x201D;). &nbsp;Therefore, the Company is subject to the reporting, information disclosure, proxy solicitation, insider trading limits and other requirements imposed on public companies by the SEC under the Exchange Act. &nbsp;This includes limits on sales of stock by certain insiders and the filing of insider ownership reports with the SEC. &nbsp;The SEC and Nasdaq have adopted regulations under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 that apply to the Company as a Nasdaq-</font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Federal Taxation</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">General. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">We are subject to federal income taxation in the same general manner as other corporations, with some exceptions discussed below. &nbsp;The following discussion of federal taxation is intended only to summarize certain pertinent federal income tax matters and is not a comprehensive description of the tax rules&nbsp;applicable to us. MutualFirst&#x2019;s federal income tax returns have been closed without audit by the IRS through its&nbsp;year ended December&nbsp;31, 2014. &nbsp;MutualFirst and MutualBank will file a consolidated federal income tax return for fiscal&nbsp;year 2018.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (&#x201C;Tax Act&#x201D;). &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">The Tax Act was enacted on December&nbsp;22, 2017 reducing the Company&#x2019;s &nbsp;federal corporate tax rate from 34% to 21%, effective January&nbsp;1, 2018. &nbsp;For deferred tax assets and liabilities, amounts were remeasured based on the rates expected to reverse in the future, which is now 21%. Based on this new law, we recorded an additional tax expense of $2.0 million due to the revaluation of the company&#x2019;s deferred tax asset in 2017. &nbsp;The Tax Act repealed the corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (&#x201C;AMT&#x201D;) and as a result a portion of the Company&#x2019;s AMT credit carryover from prior years will be refundable beginning in 2018. The effective tax rate for 2018 was 13.6% compared to 35.6% for 2017 primarily due to the reduction of the corporate tax rate to 21% and the one-time deferred tax revaluation.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Taxable Distributions and Recapture. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">Prior to 1998, bad debt reserves created prior to the&nbsp;year ended December&nbsp;31, 1997 were subject to recapture into taxable income if MutualBank failed to meet certain thrift asset and definitional tests. &nbsp;Federal legislation eliminated these thrift recapture rules. &nbsp;However, under current law, pre&#8209;1988 reserves remain subject to recapture should MutualBank make certain non-dividend distributions or cease to maintain a bank charter.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Minimum Tax. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">For tax&nbsp;years beginning after December&nbsp;31, 2018, corporate alternative minimum tax is repealed. &nbsp;The prior&nbsp;year minimum tax credit is allowed to continue to offset the taxpayer&#x2019;s regular tax liability for any tax&nbsp;year. For tax&nbsp;years beginning after 2017 and before 2022, the prior&nbsp;year minimum tax credit would be refundable in an amount equal to 50% (100% for tax&nbsp;years beginning in 2021) of the excess of the credit for the tax&nbsp;year over the amount of the credit allowable for the&nbsp;year against regular tax liability. &nbsp;MutualBank has $505,000 available as minimum tax credits for carryover, as of December&nbsp;31, 2018.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Corporate Dividends-Received Deduction. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">MutualFirst may eliminate from its income dividends received from MutualBank as a wholly owned subsidiary of MutualFirst if it elects to file a consolidated return with MutualBank. &nbsp;The corporate dividends-received deduction is 100% or 80%, in the case of dividends received from corporations with which a corporate recipient does not file a consolidated tax return, depending on the level of stock ownership of the payer of the dividend. &nbsp;Corporations which own less than 20% of the stock of a corporation distributing a dividend may deduct 50% of dividends received or accrued on their behalf.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;">Item&nbsp;1A.&nbsp;&nbsp;Risk Factors<a name="Item1ARiskFactors_74027"></a></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The following are certain risk factors that could impact our business, financial results and results of operations. Investing in our common stock involves risks, including those described below. &nbsp;These risk factors should be considered by prospective and current investors in our common stock when evaluating the disclosures in this Annual Report on Form&nbsp;10&#8209;K (particularly the forward-looking statements). &nbsp;These risk factors could cause actual results and conditions to differ materially from those projected in forward-looking statements. &nbsp;If any of the events in the following risks actually occur, or if additional risks and uncertainties not presently known to us or that we believe are immaterial do materialize, then our business, financial condition or results of operations could be materially adversely impacted. In addition, the trading price of our common stock could decline due to any of the events described in these risks.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The previous economic recession was severe in our primary market area of northern and east central Indiana, which is not a high growth market. &nbsp;A return of recessionary conditions could result in increases in our level of non-performing loans and/or reduce demand for our products and services, which could have an adverse effect on our results of operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our business activities and earnings are affected by general business conditions in the United States and in our local market area. &nbsp;These conditions are impacted by changes to short-term and long-term interest rates, inflation, unemployment levels, monetary supply, consumer confidence and spending, fluctuations in both debt and equity capital markets, and the strength of the economy in the United States generally and in our primary market area in particular. &nbsp;The economy continues to recover from the recent most severe recession, which caused high unemployment levels, declining real estate values and eroded consumer confidence. &nbsp;The recession also reduced demand for commercial business and real estate loans in our local market. &nbsp;Declines in real estate values and other effects of the recession impacted household and corporate incomes, impairing the ability of our borrowers to repay their loans in accordance with their terms and increasing our non-performing loans, loan charge-offs, provisions for loan losses and foreclosures.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Substantially all of our loans are located in Indiana, which was impacted by the recession more severely than the national average. &nbsp;Our primary market area before the Universal acquisition, which consisted of Allen, Delaware, Elkhart, Grant, Kosciusko, Randolph, St. Joseph and Wabash counties in Indiana and Berrien county in Michigan, has experienced limited population growth of 0.64% from 2000 through 2010. &nbsp;</font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">

Unemployment levels in our market areas in Indiana historically have been above the state and federal averages but have been below the state and federal level over the last three&nbsp;years. According to data published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics of the United States Department of Labor, the national unemployment rate for the United States at December&nbsp;31, 2018 was 3.7% (not seasonally adjusted) compared to an average rate of 3.1% (not seasonally adjusted) for our market areas in Indiana. 			<font style="display:inline;">A return of recessionary conditions in the domestic and international credit markets may significantly affect the markets in which we do business, the value of our loans and investments, and our ongoing operations, costs and profitability. &nbsp;Declines in real estate values and sales volumes and an increase in unemployment levels may result in higher than expected loan delinquencies and a decline in demand for our products and services. &nbsp;These negative events may cause us to incur losses and may adversely affect our capital, liquidity, and financial condition. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;">Stock prices for financial institution holding companies, including MutualFirst</font><font style="display:inline;font-style:italic;color:#000000;">, &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;">would be expected to decline substantially, and it would be significantly more difficult to raise capital or borrow in the debt markets.</font>

			<font style="display:inline;">The anticipated benefits and cost savings of the merger of&nbsp;the Company and Universal Bancorp, which was completed during the first quarter 2018, may not be realized.</font>

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The anticipated benefits and cost savings as a result of the merger, depend, in part, on our ability to continue to successfully combine the businesses of MutualFirst and Universal. &nbsp;It continues to be possible that the integration process could result in the loss of key employees or inconsistencies in standards, controls, procedures and policies that adversely affect our ability to maintain relationships with clients, customers, depositors and employees or to achieve the anticipated benefits and cost savings of the merger.&nbsp;Due to the possibility of future difficulties with the integration process, the anticipated benefits of the merger may not be realized fully or at all or may take longer to realize than expected. &nbsp;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">A substantial portion of our assets consist of various types of loans that carry varying levels of credit and interest rate risk and that are sensitive to changes in the local and national economies.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Loans Secured by Residential Property. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, $545.6 million, or 36.3% of our total loan portfolio, was secured by one-to-four family residential property, including loans held for sale and home equity loans and home equity lines of credit. &nbsp;This type of lending is generally sensitive to regional and local economic conditions that impact the ability of borrowers to meet their loan payment obligations. &nbsp;Although we continue to see recovery in the market areas we serve, the decline in residential real estate values as a result of the last downturn in the Indiana housing markets has reduced the value of the real estate collateral securing these types of loans and increased the risk that we could incur losses if borrowers default on their loans. &nbsp;In addition, borrowers seeking to sell their homes may find that they cannot sell their properties for an amount equal to or greater than the unpaid principal loan balance. &nbsp;These potential negative events may cause us to incur losses, adversely affect our capital and liquidity and damage our financial condition and business operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Commercial Real Estate, Construction and Development and Commercial Business Loans. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, $688.5 million, or 45.9% of our total loan portfolio, consisted of commercial real estate, construction and development and commercial business loans to small and mid-sized businesses, predominantly in our primary market area, which are the types of businesses that have a heightened vulnerability to local economic conditions. &nbsp;At December&nbsp;31, 2018, our loan portfolio included $53.3 million of commercial construction and development loans, $485.8 million of commercial real estate loans and $149.4 million of commercial business loans compared to $28.2 million, $318.7 million and $131.1 million for construction and development, commercial real estate and business loans, respectively, at </font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;">December&nbsp;31, 2017. &nbsp;Because we have seen growth in the credit risk of the portfolio in 2018&nbsp;primarily due to the increased&nbsp;percentage of our total loan portfolio in these types of loans, a decline in property values and other market impacts could lead to an increase in non-performing loans. &nbsp;See &#x201C;Item&nbsp;1&nbsp;- Business of MutualBank&nbsp;- Asset Quality&nbsp;- Non-Performing Assets.&#x201D;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The credit risk related to these types of loans is considered to be greater than the risk related to one-to-four family residential loans because the repayment of commercial real estate loans and commercial business loans typically is dependent on the successful operation and income stream of the borrowers&#x2019; business and the real estate securing the loans as collateral, which can be significantly affected by economic conditions. &nbsp;Any delinquent payments or the failure to repay these loans would hurt our earnings. &nbsp;Additionally, commercial loans typically involve larger loan balances to single borrowers or groups of related borrowers compared to residential real estate loans. &nbsp;Several of our commercial borrowers have more than one commercial real estate or business loan outstanding with us. &nbsp;Consequently, an adverse development with respect to one loan or one credit relationship can expose us to significantly greater risk of loss compared to an adverse development with respect to any one-to-four family residential mortgage loan. &nbsp;Finally, if we foreclose on a commercial real estate loan, our holding period for the collateral, if any, is typically longer than a one-to-four family residential property because there are fewer potential purchasers of the collateral. &nbsp;If loans that are collateralized by real estate become troubled and the value of the real estate has been significantly impaired, then we may not be able to recover the full contractual amount of principal and interest that we anticipated at the time we originated the loan, which could require us to increase our provision for loan losses and adversely affect our operating results and financial condition.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Non-Residential&nbsp;Consumer Loans</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, $267.2 million, or 17.8% of our total loan portfolio consisted of consumer loans, of which $43.7 million consisted of automobile loans, $216.6 million consisted of boat/RV loans and $6.9 million consisted of other consumer loans, including unsecured lines of credit. &nbsp;Generally, we consider these types of loans to involve a higher degree of risk compared to mortgage loans on one-to-four family, owner-occupied residential properties, particularly in the case of loans that are secured by rapidly depreciable assets, such as automobiles. &nbsp;In these cases, any repossessed collateral for a defaulted loan may not provide an adequate source of repayment of the outstanding loan balance. &nbsp;Although our indirect loans, which totaled $244.8 million at December&nbsp;31, 2018, were underwritten by a third party using our guidelines, they were primarily originated to customers outside of our normal lending area which presents greater risks than other types of lending activities. As a result of this portfolio of consumer loans, it may become necessary to increase the level of our provision for loan losses, which could negatively impact our earnings and financial condition.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;font-style:italic;">Adjustable Rate Loans</font><font style="display:inline;font-weight:bold;">. &nbsp;</font><font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, $743.9 million, or 49.6% of our total loan portfolio consisted of adjustable rate loans. &nbsp;Borrowers with adjustable rate loans are exposed to increased&nbsp;monthly payments when the related interest rate adjusts upward under the terms of the loan to the rate computed in accordance with the applicable index and margin. &nbsp;Any rise in prevailing market interest rates may result in increased payments for borrowers who have adjustable-rate loans, increasing the possibility of default. &nbsp;Borrowers seeking to avoid these increased&nbsp;monthly payments by refinancing their loans may no longer be able to find available replacement loans at comparable or lower interest rates. &nbsp;In addition, declining real estate prices may prevent refinancing or a sale of the property, because borrowers have insufficient equity in the real estate. &nbsp;These events, alone or in combination, may contribute to higher delinquency rates and negatively impact our earnings.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">If our allowance for loan losses is not sufficient to cover actual loan losses or our non-performing assets increase, our earnings will suffer. &nbsp;Increases in our provision for loan losses adversely impact our earnings and operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">We make various assumptions and judgments about the collectability of our loan portfolio, including the creditworthiness of our borrowers and the value of the real estate and other assets serving as collateral. &nbsp;</font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;">35</font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#TOC"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</font></a>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;">In determining the amount of the allowance for loan losses, we review our loans and our loss and delinquency experience and evaluate current economic conditions. &nbsp;Management recognizes that significant new growth in loan portfolios, new loan products and the refinancing of existing loans can result in portfolios comprised of unseasoned loans that may not perform in a historical or projected manner. &nbsp;If our assumptions are incorrect, our allowance for loan losses may not be sufficient to cover actual losses, resulting in additions to our allowance. &nbsp;Additions to our allowance decrease our net income. &nbsp;Our regulators periodically review our allowance for loan losses and may require us to recognize additions to the allowance based on their judgments about information available to them at the time of their review. &nbsp;These increases in our allowance for loan losses or loan charge-offs may have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations. &nbsp;Our allowance for loan losses was 0.89% of gross loans and 145.85% of non-performing loans at December&nbsp;31, 2018, compared to 1.05% of gross loans and 235.90% of non-performing loans at December&nbsp;31, 2017 and 1.06% of gross loans and 230.99% of non-performing loans at December&nbsp;31, 2016.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, our non-performing assets (which consist of non-accrual loans, loans 90&nbsp;days delinquent and still accruing, non-accrual troubled debt restructurings, foreclosed real estate and other repossessed assets) totaled $11.1 million, which was an&nbsp;increase of $5.1 million, or an&nbsp;85.8% &nbsp;increase in non-performing assets from December&nbsp;31, 2017. &nbsp;This increase&nbsp;was primarily due a $1.0 million increase in real estate owned as a result of the&nbsp;acquisition of Universal and an increase in non-performing loans primarily as the result of a $3.2 million commercial real estate loan not performing. &nbsp;Our non-performing assets adversely affect our net income in various ways. &nbsp;We do not record interest income on non-accrual loans or real estate owned. &nbsp;We must reserve for estimated credit losses, which are established through a current period charge to the provision for loan losses, and from time to time, if appropriate, we must write down the value of properties in our real estate owned (&#x201C;REO&#x201D;) portfolio to reflect changing market values. &nbsp;Additionally, there are legal fees associated with the resolution of problem assets as well as carrying costs including taxes, insurance and maintenance related to our REO. &nbsp;Further, the resolution of non-performing assets requires the active involvement of management, potentially distracting them from the overall supervision of our operations and other income-producing activities.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">During 2018, we recorded a provision for loan losses of $2.1 million compared to $1.2 million in 2017 and $850,000 in 2016. &nbsp;We also recorded net loan charge-offs of $1.2 million in 2018, compared to $1.2 million in 2017 and $1.1 million in 2016. &nbsp;The increase in provision for loan losses was primarily due to our growing loan portfolio and our need to support the existing loan portfolio mix with commercial and non-real estate consumer loans making up 63.7% of the loan portfolio at the end of 2018 compared to 57.0% at the end of 2017. &nbsp;We did not experience declining trends in the housing, real estate and local business markets; however, if that would return, we would expect increased levels of delinquencies and credit losses to return, which would adversely impact our financial condition and results of operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">The Financial Accounting Standards Board, or FASB, adopted Accounting Standards Update, or ASU, No. 2016-13 &#x201C;Financial Instruments&#x2014;Credit Losses (Topic 326): Measurement of Credit Losses on Financial Instruments,&#x201D; or CECL, on June 16, 2016, which changed the loss model to take into account current expected credit losses. This accounting pronouncement is expected to be applicable to us effective for our fiscal year beginning January 1, 2020.&nbsp;&nbsp;The federal banking regulators, including the Federal Reserve and the FDIC, have adopted a rule that gives a banking organization the option to phase in over a three-year period the day-one adverse effects of CECL on its regulatory capital. </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">CECL substantially changes how we calculate our allowance for loan and lease losses. We are evaluating CECL and when we will be required to adopt it. We cannot predict when and how it will affect our results of operations and financial condition, including our regulatory capital.&nbsp; </font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;">36</font>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 30pt;color:#0563C1;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<a href="#TOC"><font style="display:inline;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;color:#0563C1;">Table of Contents</font></a>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Changes in interest rates could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our results of operations and financial condition are affected significantly by changes in interest rates. &nbsp;Our results of operations depend substantially on our net interest income, which is the difference between the interest income we earn on our interest-earning assets, such as loans and securities, and the interest expense we pay on our interest-bearing liabilities, such as deposits and borrowings. &nbsp;Because interest-bearing liabilities generally reprice or mature more quickly than interest-earning assets, an increase in interest rates generally would tend to result in a decrease in net interest income.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Changes in interest rates also may affect the average life of loans and mortgage-related securities. &nbsp;Decreases in interest rates or continuing low interest rates can result in increased prepayments of loans and mortgage-related securities, as borrowers refinance to reduce their borrowing costs. &nbsp;Under these circumstances, we have been and continue to be subject to reinvestment risk to the extent that we are unable to reinvest the cash received from such prepayments at rates that are comparable to the rates on existing loans and securities. &nbsp;Additionally, increases in interest rates may decrease loan demand and make it more difficult for borrowers to repay adjustable-rate loans. &nbsp;Also, increases in interest rates may extend the life of fixed-rate assets, which could limit the funds we have available to reinvest in higher-yielding alternatives, and may result in customers withdrawing certificates of deposit early so long as the early withdrawal penalty is less than the interest they could receive as a result of the higher market interest rates.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Changes in interest rates also affect the current fair value of our interest-earning securities portfolio. &nbsp;Generally, the value of securities moves inversely with changes in interest rates. &nbsp;At December&nbsp;31, 2018, the fair value of our portfolio of available for sale securities totaled $370.9 million. &nbsp;Gross unrealized gains on these securities totaled $2.5 million, while gross unrealized losses on these securities totaled $5.6 million, resulting in a net unrealized loss of $3.2 million at December&nbsp;31, 2018.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">At December&nbsp;31, 2018, our interest rate risk analysis indicated that our net portfolio value would decrease by 12.9% if there was an instantaneous parallel 200 basis point increase in market interest rates. &nbsp;See &#x201C;Management&#x2019;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operation&nbsp;- Asset/Liability Management.&#x201D;</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our strategies to modify our interest rate risk profile may be difficult to implement.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our asset/liability management strategies are designed to minimize our interest rate risk sensitivity. One such strategy is to increase the amount of adjustable rate and/or short-term assets. The Bank offers adjustable rate loan products as a means to achieve this strategy. The recent availability of lower rates on fixed-rate loans has generally created a decrease in borrower demand for adjustable rate assets. Additionally, these adjustable-rate assets may prepay. Despite this, at December&nbsp;31, 2018, 49.6% of our loan portfolio consisted of adjustable-rate loans, compared to 45.0% at December&nbsp;31, 2017.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">We also are managing our liabilities to moderate our interest rate risk sensitivity. &nbsp;Customer demand is primarily for short-term certificates of deposit and transaction accounts. &nbsp;Using short-term liabilities to fund long-term, fixed-rate assets will increase the interest rate sensitivity of any financial institution. &nbsp;When needed, we are utilizing FHLB advances agreements to mitigate the impact of customer demand by lengthening the maturities of these advances or entering into longer term repurchase agreements, depending on liquidity or investment opportunities.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">FHLB advances are entered into as liquidity is needed or to fund assets that provide for a spread considered sufficient by management. &nbsp;If we are unable to originate adjustable rate assets at favorable rates or fund loan originations or securities purchases with long-term advances or structured borrowings, we may have difficulty executing this asset/liability management strategy and/or it may result in a reduction in profitability.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">

			<font style="display:inline;">37</font>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">OTTI charges in our investment securities portfolio could result in losses and adversely affect our continuing operations. &nbsp;Our securities portfolio may be negatively impacted by fluctuations in market value and interest rates, which may have an adverse effect on our financial condition.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our securities portfolio may be impacted by fluctuations in market value, potentially reducing accumulated other comprehensive income and/or earnings, which may materially adversely affect our stockholders&#x2019; equity, regulatory capital and continuing operations. &nbsp;Fluctuations in market value may be caused by changes&nbsp;in interest rates, lower market prices for securities and limited investor demand, as well as the default rates of specific financial institutions whose securities provide the underlying collateral for these securities and changes in credit risk based on the condition of the issuer. &nbsp;The valuation of our investment securities also is influenced by the implementation of Securities and Exchange Commission and Financial Accounting Standards Board guidance on fair value accounting, which requires us to report our available for sale securities at their estimated fair value. &nbsp;Our stockholders&#x2019; equity is periodically adjusted by the amount of change in the estimated fair value of the available for sale securities, net of taxes. &nbsp;At December&nbsp;31, 2018, the change in unrealized gains on securities available for sale from the level at December&nbsp;31, 2017 was a decrease of $2.1 million. When OTTI is present, the market environment more likely than not limits our ability to mitigate our exposure to valuation changes in these securities by selling them.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our securities portfolio is evaluated for OTTI on at least a quarterly basis. &nbsp;If this evaluation shows impairment to the actual or projected cash flows associated with one or more securities, a potential loss to earnings may occur. &nbsp;We have not recorded any OTTI since 2011. &nbsp;As of December&nbsp;31, 2018, we have no securities that are deemed impaired.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">If our investments in real estate are not properly valued or sufficiently reserved for to cover actual losses, or if we are required to increase our valuation reserves, our earnings could be reduced.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">We obtain updated valuations in the form of appraisals and broker price opinions when a loan has been foreclosed and the property taken in as REO, and at certain other times during the assets holding period. &nbsp;Our net book value (&#x201C;NBV&#x201D;) in the loan at the time of foreclosure and thereafter is compared to the updated market value of the foreclosed property less estimated selling costs (fair value). &nbsp;A charge-off is recorded for any excess in the asset&#x2019;s NBV over its fair value. &nbsp;If our valuation process is incorrect, the fair value of our investments in real estate may not be sufficient to recover our NBV in such assets, resulting in the need for additional charge-offs. &nbsp;Additional material charge-offs to our investments in real estate could have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations. &nbsp;Our regulators periodically review our REO and may require us to recognize further charge-offs. &nbsp;Any increase in our charge-offs, as required by our regulator, may have a material adverse effect on our financial condition and results of operations.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">We face risks related to covenants in our loan sales to investors and secondary mortgage market conditions.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-bottom:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our agreements with investors to sell our loans generally contain covenants that require us to repurchase loans under certain circumstances, including some delinquencies, or to return premiums paid by those investors if the loans are paid off early. &nbsp;If we are required to repurchase sold loans under these covenants, they may be deemed troubled loans, with the potential for charge-offs and/or loss provision changes, which could impact our earnings and asset quality ratios adversely. &nbsp;The Bank was not required to repurchase any loans from investors during 2018 or 2017.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;border-top:1pt none #D9D9D9 ;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Our ability to sell loans on the secondary mortgage market is impacted by interest rate changes and investor demand or expected return. If this market becomes less liquid, we may not be able to rely as much on loan sales to reduce our interest rate and credit risk.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;"></font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><p style="margin:0pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;"><font style="display:inline;"></font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">We use estimates in determining the fair value of certain assets, such as mortgage servicing rights (&#x201C;MSRs&#x201D;). &nbsp;If our estimates prove to be incorrect, we may be required to write down the value of these assets which could adversely affect our earnings.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">We sell a portion of our one-to-four family loans in the secondary market. &nbsp;We generally retain the right to service these loans through the Bank. &nbsp;At December&nbsp;31, 2018, the book value of our MSRs was $2.7 million. &nbsp;We use a financial model that uses, wherever possible, quoted market prices to value our MSRs. &nbsp;This model is complex and also uses assumptions related to interest and discount rates, prepayment speeds, delinquency and foreclosure rates and ancillary fee income. &nbsp;Valuations are highly dependent upon the reasonableness of our assumptions and the predictability of the relationships that drive the results of the model. &nbsp;The primary risk associated with MSRs is that they will lose a substantial portion of their value as a result of higher than anticipated prepayments occasioned by declining interest rates. &nbsp;Conversely, these assets generally increase in value in a rising interest rate environment to the extent that prepayments are slower than anticipated. &nbsp;If prepayment speeds increase more than estimated or delinquency and default levels are higher than anticipated we may be required to write down the value of our MSRs which could have a material adverse effect on our net income and capital levels. &nbsp;The Company obtains independent valuations at least semi-annually to determine if impairment in the asset exists.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">Declining economic conditions may adversely impact the fees generated by our asset management and trust business.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">To the extent our asset management and trust clients and their assets become adversely impacted by weak economic and stock market conditions, they may choose to withdraw the assets managed by us and/or the value of their assets may decline. Our asset management revenues are based on the value of the assets we manage. If our clients withdraw assets or the value of their assets decline, our revenues from these activities may be adversely affected. These fees totaled $3.9 million and $4.0 million in 2018 and 2017, respectively.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-weight:bold;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;color:#000000;">We face significant operational and reputational risks. &nbsp;As a </font><font style="display:inline;">community bank, maintaining our reputation in our market area is critical to the success of our business, and the failure to do so may materially adversely affect our performance. &nbsp;Our business may be adversely affected by an increasing prevalence of fraud and other financial crimes impacting the banking industry.</font>
		</p>
		<p style="margin:0pt 0pt 12pt;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">
			<font style="display:inline;">We are a community bank, and our reputation is one of the most valuable components of our business. &nbsp;A key component of our business strategy is to rely on our reputation for customer service and knowledge of local markets to expand our presence by capturing new business opportunities from existing and prospective customers in our current market and contiguous areas. &nbsp;As such, we strive to conduct our business in a manner that enhances our reputation. &nbsp;This is done, in part, by recruiting, hiring and retaining employees who share our core values of being an integral part of the communities we serve, delivering superior service to our customers and caring about our customers and associates. &nbsp;We operate in many different financial service businesses and rely on the ability of our employees and systems to process a significant number of transactions. &nbsp;Operational risk is the risk of loss from operations, including fraud by employees or outside persons, employees&#x2019; execution of incorrect or unauthorized transactions, data processing and technology errors or hacking and breaches of internal control systems. &nbsp;If our reputation is negatively affected, by the actions of our employees, by our inability to conduct our operations in a manner that is appealing to current or prospective customers, or otherwise, our business and, therefore, our operating results may be materially adversely affected. &nbsp;Our loans to businesses and individuals and our deposit relationships and related transactions are subject to exposure to the risk of loss due to </font><font style="display:inline;color:#000000;">fraud</font><font style="display:inline;"> and other financial crimes. &nbsp;Nationally, reported incidents of fraud and other financial crimes have increased. &nbsp;We have experienced an increase in losses due to apparent fraud and other financial crimes. &nbsp;Our policies and procedures designed to prevent such losses may not prevent all such losses. &nbsp;The Company continues to evaluate and implement new technologies; including, but not limited </font></p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;">
		<p><font size="1"> </font></p><div style="width:100%">

		<p style="margin:24pt 0pt 0pt;text-align:center;font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif;font-size: 10pt;">

			<font style="display:inline;">39</font>

		</p>

</div></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><hr align="center" style='background-color:#000000; border-width:0; color:#000000; height:2pt; lineheight:0; width:100%;'></hr><p style="page-break-after:always">&nbsp;</p></div><div style="margin-left:11.7647058823529%;margin-right:11.7647058823529%;"><div style="width:100%">
